ety.text: Old French favorbor. Middle English favour English favor From Middle English favour, favor, faver, from Anglo-Norman favour, from mainland Old French favor, from Latin favor (“good will; kindness; partiality”), from faveō (“to be kind to”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂weh₁yeti (“to be favourable to”), from the root Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to shine, glow light”). Respelled in American English to more closely match its Latin etymon. Compare also Danish favør (“favor”), Irish fabhar (“favor”), from the same Romance source.

senses.d: A kind or helpful deed; an instance of voluntarily assisting (someone).
ex: He did me a favor when he took the time to drive me home.

senses.d: Goodwill; benevolent regard.
ex: She enjoyed the queen's favor.
to fall out of favor

senses.d: A small gift; a party favor.
ex: wedding favor
At the holiday dinner, the hosts had set a favor by each place setting.

senses.d: Mildness or mitigation of punishment; lenity.
ex: I could not discover the lenity and favour of this sentence.

senses.d: The object of regard; person or thing favoured.
ex: All these his wondrous works, but chiefly man, / His chief delight and favour.

senses.d: Appearance; look; countenance; face.
ex: This boy is fair, of female favour.

senses.d: Partiality; bias
A letter, a written communication.
ex: I will now take some notice of your last favour; but being so far behind-hand with you, must be brief.

senses.d: A resemblance, likeness.
Anything worn publicly as a pledge of a woman's favor.
To look upon fondly; to prefer.
ex: And the angel came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favored, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women.

senses.d: To use more often.
ex: […] alone, without having to favor his right, uninjured leg, […]

senses.d: To encourage, conduce to
To do a favor [noun sense 1] for; to show beneficence toward.
ex: Would you favor us with a poetry reading?

senses.d: To resemble; especially, to look like (another person).
ex: I thought—it doesn't matter—you seemed to favour your ma,
You’re complected like your pa. He had red hair. But you favor your ma in your eyes and mouth.

senses.d: To treat or use (something) gently
ex: I always try to favor my bad knee.

ety.text: Attested from the 1580s, borrowed from Middle French favorit, from Old French favorit or Italian favorito (“favoured, favourite”), past participle of Italian favorire (“to favor”), from favore, from Latin favor (“good will, favor”), from the verb faveō (“to favour”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂weh₁yeti (“to be favourable to”), from the root Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to shine, glow light”). Doublet of favori.

senses.d: Most-liked. (In other words, [person]'s favorite [noun] = the [noun] that [person] likes the most.)
ex: This is my favourite day!
I saw a hilariously funny movie with all of my favourite comedians in it.

senses.d: Liked, cherished.
ex: What joy has this dog in miſchief!—More than I can have in the completion of my moſt favourite purpoſes!

senses.d: A person or thing who enjoys special regard or favour.
ex: The teacher's favourite always went first.

senses.d: A person who is preferred or trusted above all others.
A contestant or competitor thought most likely to win.
ex: You were my favourite to win the spelling competition.
She's the favourite, she'll probably be elected.

senses.d: A bookmark on a web browser or website.
A short curl dangling over the temples, fashionable in the reign of Charles II.
ex: the Favourites hang loose upon the Temples with a languishing Lock in the middle

senses.d: To favour.
To bookmark.
To add to one's list of favourite items on a website that allows users to compile such lists.

ety.text: From Middle French favori, favorit (16th c.), from Italian favorito, past participle of favorire (“to favour”). The form in -it was borrowed directly from the Italian participle, while that in -i (feminine accordingly favorie) is in line with the Middle French verb favorir (now replaced with favoriser).
Borrowed from Italian favorito. Compare English favorite/favourite.
From Middle English favourable, from Old French favorable, from Latin favōrābilis, from favor. By surface analysis, favour + -able.

senses.d: Apt to win favour; pleasing.
ex: The candidate wearing the business suit made a favourable impression.

senses.d: Expressing or indicating favour or goodwill; approving, encouraging.
ex: The proposal has received many favourable comments.

senses.d: Useful or helpful.
ex: We made quick progress, due to favourable winds.

So draw him home to those that mourn
⁠In vain; a favourable speed
⁠Ruffle thy mirror’d mast, and lead
Thro’ prosperous floods his holy urn.

senses.d: Convenient or at a suitable time; opportune.
ex: The rain stopped at a favourable time for our tennis match.

senses.d: Auspicious or lucky.
ex: She says that she was born under a favourable star.

senses.d: Treated or regarded with partiality.
Having a certain appearance or physical features.
ex: ill-favoured; well-favoured; hard-favoured

senses.d: Wearing a favour.
ex: a white-favoured footman
